prize_parts.citation: for evidence on how exposure to import competition and technological change reshapes labour demand, local labour markets and wages, and on the persistent costs of adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from the end of round 1: B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, as a single part. What I tested in this round was whether the case rests on the support count or on the substance. I rest it on the substance. The work asks a first-order question about who bears the adjustment costs of trade and technology. It uses transparent local-labour-market designs that others could attack, and they did. The robust finding is that exposure produced concentrated and persistent local adjustment costs. That finding survived critiques of the shift-share instruments, the exposure measures and the persistence estimates, while magnitudes were refined. That is the record I want before a prize. The attribution is also the tightest of the shortlisted entries I know well: the empirical programme is jointly authored by the three named people. I have kept the citation on exposure, labour demand, local labour markets and wages, and on persistent adjustment costs. It makes no claim about an elasticity and does not purport to credit the whole task-based theory. That answers the chair's wording question. Wage inequality is not named in the citation, because the evidence is strongest on local employment and wages and I do not want the wording to claim more than the credited work shows. I would still want the Committee to read the shift-share and persistence critiques before the private vote. Taking my 2023 presentation as context and not as a preference, I judge the entry only by the criteria I apply to the others.
statement.case_against: The ballot entry bundles two strands, the task and skill-bias framework and the China-shock evidence. A trio built on the trade-shock papers gives the technology strand only partial credit. It leaves out Katz, whose work on the race between education and technology is foundational, and Levy and Murnane. Acemoglu, who was recognised in 2024, shares part of the task framework. I cannot say precisely what the task strand adds beyond work recognised in 2023 and 2024, and the chair's question on this remains open for me. I accept the cost of leaving Katz out because I cannot defend a mixed citation with a three-name cap. The size and long-run persistence of the effects, the shift-share identification and the split between trade and automation are all still debated. The 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes may also reduce the Committee's appetite for another labour-and-technology award. If the Committee judges the entry too composite, B003 is my fallback, because it also pairs a framework with credible identification.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 with Helpman and Melitz. She reads the record on the China shock as more mixed than 'held up', and she sees the task framework as overlapping with 2024 recognition. She regards B034 as less exposed on magnitudes and recent adjacent prizes.
responses.response: I accept that the debate over exposure measures, persistence and automation is real, and I have worded the citation to avoid a settled magnitude. I would separate the question of how large the effects are from the question of whether the central finding, persistent local adjustment costs, has survived re-examination. I read the follow-up work as having refined the first and not overturned the second. I agree that B034 is a mature and conceptually clean achievement, and I do not dispute its attribution to Melitz and Helpman. The Krugman overlap and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question seem to me no smaller than the 2024 overlap is for B036. I therefore do not read the objections as separating the two cases decisively. I have not changed my choice, but I would not regard B034 as a weak outcome.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B020 and ranks B036 seventh. He doubts the maturity bar is met because of the continuing dispute over identification, persistence and magnitude, though he says he would not oppose it.
responses.response: The identification question is the right one, and I would like the Committee to review the shift-share critiques directly instead of assuming they are answered. I do not think the dispute counts against maturity. The core papers are more than a decade old, and the later work on persistence tested them. A central result that survives in qualified form after hostile re-examination is mature in the sense that matters. I also disagree that structural demand estimation is more verifiable. Its estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, as you say yourself. B020 is also a methods contribution with a real attribution problem between demand estimation and dynamic oligopoly. I value its reach into antitrust, but I do not see it as the cleaner case.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B034 and now says that if B036 were preferred he would propose Autor, Dorn and Hanson, but he keeps B034 ahead on cleaner credit and the unresolved persistence debate.
responses.response: I am glad you moved to the Autor-Dorn-Hanson attribution, which settles the Katz question among most of us. I would resist the idea that B034's credit is cleaner. By your own account, the priority issue with Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum cannot be settled on the evidence supplied. On B036 the authorship of the central papers is not in doubt, and the live debate is about magnitudes. The Committee can state that debate in the citation's scope. I agree that a Melitz-style selection mechanism is distinct from what the 2008 prize recognised. That is why I would treat B034 as a legitimate alternative and not weigh it down with that overlap.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues the citation should be anchored on empirical evidence about trade and labour-market adjustment and not on a general theory of technology, because the task framework has originators outside the entry.
responses.response: I agree with the anchoring, and my citation follows it. I would still keep technological change in the wording, because Autor's work links the exposure evidence to technology and the Committee would be misdescribing the programme if it named only trade. Naming technological change as an object of the evidence does not credit the task theory. I also take your point that B010 is a weaker alternative for attribution because Rogerson is outside the credited names. I keep B010 as my second alternative because its impact on development accounting is large. I recognise that its credit structure is less stable than B036's, and Boppart's disclosed tie to Klenow means it should not gain from his ranking.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B018 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He treats B036 as a close alternative and keeps B018 ahead because the New Keynesian work is four decades old, fully tested and has little overlap with the 2022 prize. He concedes that credit is spread across at least eight contributors.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific importance or maturity of the New Keynesian framework. My difficulty is the one you name: credit is spread over at least eight people, and any trio omits Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose work made the framework operational. A founding-contribution citation could be drafted around Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, but I cannot tell whether the Committee could defend that cut as discovery and not as selection. By contrast the credit for B036 is jointly authored and does not need that judgment. This is the reason I weight attribution as heavily as I do. It is not a verdict on the field.

uncertainties: How far the shift-share exposure critiques and the persistence evidence change the case for a lasting discovery, and whether the Committee will review them before the vote. A finding that the central result depends on one instrument would lower my support.

Whether the Committee prefers a narrower trade-shock citation or a broader labour-and-technology citation that would bring Katz and the task lineage back, and whether the three-name cap makes that second option impossible to credit cleanly.
What the task and technology strand adds beyond work recognised in 2023 and 2024, given that some of its originators (Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane) are outside the credited set.
Whether the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes leave room for another labour-and-technology award.
Whether B034 would be the cleaner outcome if the priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum can be answered, which I cannot resolve from the supplied evidence.
My assessment draws on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied committee materials, and I have not independently verified any attribution claim.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My profile shows no collaboration or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or the other credited names on B003 and B010, and my frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not on the shortlist. My field of labour economics is adjacent to the preferred entry, and I disclose that without treating it as a conflict. I presented the 2023 prize, which I treat as context and not as a voting preference. I have noted Boppart's disclosed tie to Klenow in assessing B010 and have not relied on his view of it. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
